questions.q: Which two properties make a problem a good fit for dynamic programming?
questions.explain: Without overlap, plain recursion or divide and conquer is enough. Without optimal substructure, combining best sub-answers does not give the best answer. DP needs both.
options: It is sorted, and it has no duplicates
Optimal substructure (the best answer is built from best answers to subproblems) and overlapping subproblems (the same subproblems come up many times)
It is recursive, and it has a base case
It is greedy, and it is fast

questions.q: Merge sort also splits a problem into subproblems. Why is it divide and conquer rather than dynamic programming?
questions.explain: DP pays off when the recursion reaches the same subproblem repeatedly. Merge sort's halves share no items, so caching their answers would never produce a hit.
options: Because it sorts
Its subproblems (the two halves) never overlap, so there is nothing to remember and reuse
Because it uses recursion
Because it is O(n log n)

questions.q: How many calls does the plain recursive Fibonacci make for fib(5)?
questions.explain: fib(5) calls fib(4) and fib(3); fib(4) calls fib(3) again, and so on. The call tree has 15 nodes for only 6 distinct subproblems (fib(0) to fib(5)).

questions.q: The same function with a memo. What does it print?
questions.explain: Each fib(k) for k from 2 to 10 is computed once (9 memo entries). Each of those makes two calls, and the second call is always a cache hit or a base case: 1 + 2 × 9 = 19 calls, instead of 177 without the memo.

questions.q: How do you estimate the running time of a dynamic programming solution?
questions.explain: Every state is computed once. Coin change has amount + 1 states and does one check per denomination in each: O(amount × d). Knapsack has (n + 1) × (C + 1) states with O(1) work each.
options: 2 to the power of the number of inputs
The number of distinct states multiplied by the work done per state
The depth of the recursion
The size of the largest input value

questions.q: The van problem has 20 parcels and 200 kg of capacity. How many distinct subproblems best(i, room) can there be at most?
questions.explain: i ranges from 0 to 20 and room from 0 to 200. The plain search makes over a million calls, but only these 4,221 questions are different: that gap is the overlap DP removes.

questions.q: What is memoization in dynamic programming?
questions.explain: Memoization is top-down: the recursion drives the order, and the cache ensures each state is computed once. Filling a table from the bottom is tabulation.
options: Writing the recurrence down in comments
Keeping the natural recursive function and adding a cache: look up an answer before computing it, store it after
Filling a table from the smallest subproblems up
Keeping only the last two rows of a table

questions.q: When filling a DP table bottom-up, what must be true about the order?
questions.explain: That is the whole job of the loop order. For coin change, fewest[a] reads smaller amounts, so amounts go upwards. The transport-pass table reads later days, so it is filled backwards from the last day.
options: Cells must be filled in random order
Every cell must be filled after all the cells it depends on
The largest subproblems must come first
Each row must be filled right to left

questions.q: A DP has a chain of 200,000 states, each depending on the previous one. Why prefer tabulation over memoization here?
questions.explain: Both compute the same values. The recursion depth of memoization equals the longest chain of dependent states. Tabulation replaces the call stack with a loop.
options: Memoization gives wrong answers for long chains
Memoized recursion would be 200,000 calls deep and overflow the call stack; a loop over a table has no depth limit
Tabulation always uses less memory
Maps cannot hold 200,000 entries

questions.q: When can memoization do less work than tabulation?
questions.explain: A table computes every cell. The recursion only follows the dependencies of the question asked. If most cells are irrelevant, top-down can be much cheaper.
options: Never; they always do the same work
When many states in the full table are never reached from the starting question, because memoization only computes the states the recursion actually visits
When the table is small
When the answer is 0

questions.q: What does this tabulation print?
questions.explain: This counts the ways to climb n stairs one or two at a time: ways[n] = ways ending with a one-step plus ways ending with a two-step. Starting from [1, 1] (one way to climb 0 or 1 stairs), the table for 0 to 6 has seven entries.

questions.q: Each Fibonacci entry depends only on the previous two. What does that allow?
questions.explain: The time is still O(n), one step per entry. Only the memory shrinks. The same idea keeps one or two rows of a knapsack or LCS table when you only need the final value.
options: Computing fib(n) in O(1) time
Keeping two variables instead of the whole table: O(1) memory instead of O(n)
Skipping the base cases
Computing the entries in any order

questions.q: fib(79) computed with ordinary numbers gives a value that looks fine. What is the problem?
questions.explain: Numbers above 253 − 1 cannot represent every integer, and arithmetic on them rounds without warning. fib(78) is the last Fibonacci number that is safe. Check with Number.isSafeInteger.
options: There is none
It exceeds Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, so it may be silently rounded; use BigInt for large exact integers
JavaScript throws a RangeError
It returns Infinity

questions.q: In the coin change table, what is fewest[0], and why does it matter?
questions.explain: A wrong base case shifts every answer. With fewest[0] = 1, every amount would come out one piece too high.
options: Infinity, because nothing can be paid with no coins
1, because at least one coin is needed
0: paying nothing needs no coins, and every other entry is built on it (for example fewest[400] = 1 + fewest[0])
It is never used

questions.q: Why does the coin change table use Infinity for amounts that cannot be made?
questions.explain: With -1 or null, 1 + fewest[a - v] would produce 0 or 1 and look like a great option. Convert Infinity to "impossible" only when returning to the caller.
options: Because JavaScript arrays default to Infinity
1 + Infinity is still Infinity and Math.min ignores it whenever a real option exists, so impossible amounts never win a comparison
To make the table larger
Because null cannot be stored in an array

questions.q: Coins of 1, 3 and 4. What does this print?
questions.explain: DP finds 3 + 3 (2 coins). Greedy takes 4 first and then needs 1 + 1 (3 coins). DP tries every coin as the last one for every amount, so it cannot be tricked by a tempting first choice.

questions.q: The table fewest[a] tells you how many notes, but not which. What is the usual way to recover the notes?
questions.explain: The choice table records the decision made at each state, like parent links in BFS. Walking back costs O(number of notes).
options: Run greedy on the amount
Store, for each amount, the note that achieved the minimum (a choice table); start at the target, read the note, subtract it, and repeat until 0
Search every combination with that many notes
Sort the denominations

questions.q: What does this reconstruction print?
questions.explain: ₦1,300 needs three vouchers. For 1,300, the value 500 is tried first and reaches the minimum (1 + fewest[800] = 3); 400 only ties, and the check is strictly less than, so 500 is recorded. The walk then reads the choice for 800, which is 400, and for 400, which is 400. There is no ₦200 voucher, so the second option is impossible.

questions.q: Counting the ways to pay an amount, one version loops over denominations outside and amounts inside; another loops over amounts outside and denominations inside. What is the difference?
questions.explain: With denominations in the outer loop, each combination is built in one fixed order of denominations, so it is counted once. With amounts outside, every order of choosing is a separate path. Decide which question the business is asking.
options: None; they give the same number
Denominations outside counts combinations (₦400 + ₦100 once); amounts outside counts sequences (₦400 then ₦100, and ₦100 then ₦400, separately)
Amounts outside is faster
Denominations outside counts only the fewest-piece ways

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: As combinations, 4 = 1+1+1+1, 1+1+2 or 2+2: 3 ways. As sequences, 1+1+2 can be ordered 3 ways (112, 121, 211), giving 1 + 3 + 1 = 5.

questions.q: In best[i][c] = max(best[i − 1][c], fee + best[i − 1][c − kg]), what do the two options mean?
questions.explain: Every 0/1 decision is "skip or take". Taking it uses room, so the rest must fit in c − kg. Both options only look at row i − 1, which is why each parcel is used at most once.
options: Take the parcel twice, or once
Leave parcel i (the best from the earlier parcels with the same room), or take it (its fee plus the best from the earlier parcels with kg less room)
Put the parcel in the front or the back of the van
Sort by fee, or sort by weight

questions.q: A 5 kg bag, whole items only. What does this print?
questions.explain: Row 2 (phone and laptop) reaches ₦150,000 from 4 kg up (both fit). With the speaker, phone + speaker (5 kg, ₦160,000) beats phone + laptop. All three together would be 8 kg, too heavy.

questions.q: The knapsack table works well with capacity in kilograms. Someone switches all weights to grams. What happens?
questions.explain: O(n × C) depends on the numeric value C, not on how many inputs there are. Choose the coarsest unit the business allows, and validate the capacity before allocating a table.
options: Nothing changes; Big O is the same
The table becomes 1,000 times larger for the same van, because the running time and memory grow with the capacity value (pseudo-polynomial)
The answers become wrong
It becomes faster because the numbers are more precise

questions.q: In the one-row knapsack, why must the capacity loop go down from the capacity to the parcel's weight?
questions.explain: Going up solves the unbounded knapsack, where each item can be taken many times. With a 0/1 van it silently reports impossible loads, such as one 50 kg parcel earning four times its fee.
options: Because it is faster
Going down, best[c − kg] still holds the value from before this parcel, so the parcel is used at most once; going up, it may already include this parcel, allowing repeats
Because arrays must be read backwards
It does not matter

questions.q: One parcel of 2 kg worth ₦3,000, a 6 kg van. What does this print?
questions.explain: Going down, each cell reads a value from before this parcel: at most one parcel, ₦3,000. Going up, best[2] is updated first and then reused by best[4] and best[6]: three copies of the same parcel.

questions.q: The one-row knapsack uses O(C) memory instead of O(n × C). What do you lose?
questions.explain: The walk back needs to compare best[i][c] with best[i − 1][c]. With one row, those values are gone. Keep the full table (or a compact record of decisions) when you need the list.
options: Correctness of the best value
The ability to reconstruct which parcels were taken, because the earlier rows are overwritten
The ability to handle parcels heavier than the van
Nothing at all

questions.q: What is the difference between a subsequence and a substring of "PAYMENT"?
questions.explain: The LCS of two texts allows gaps, which is what lets a diff keep all unchanged lines even when lines are inserted or deleted between them.
options: They are the same thing
A substring is contiguous ("YMEN"); a subsequence keeps order but may skip letters ("PMT")
A subsequence must be at the start
A substring may reorder letters

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both words start with TRANS. After that, TRANSFER has F, E, R and TRANSACTION has A, C, T, I, O, N: no letter in common, so the LCS is 5. ORDER appears inside REORDER in order (5, not 7: the LCS cannot be longer than the shorter text). No common letters gives 0.

questions.q: What does this diff print?
questions.explain: The LCS is rice, salt. Oil appears only in the old list (deleted), sugar only in the new one (inserted). Keeping the LCS as long as possible gives the smallest diff; the third option is a valid but useless diff that keeps nothing.
options: =rice -oil =salt +sugar
=rice +salt -oil -salt +sugar
-rice -oil -salt +rice +salt +sugar
=rice -oil +sugar =salt

questions.q: Why don't tools like git use the plain LCS table to diff two versions of a 100,000-line file?
questions.explain: O(n × m) time and memory is fine for a delivery note, not for large files. Myers' algorithm runs in O((n + m) × d) for d differences.
options: LCS gives wrong diffs for large files
The table would have about 10 billion cells; git uses algorithms such as Myers', whose cost grows with the number of differences, so nearly identical files are fast
Because git compares bytes, not lines
Because LCS cannot handle deletions

questions.q: For "did you mean" suggestions, the edit distance between "sneekers" and "sneakers" is 1. What does the edit distance measure?
questions.explain: One replacement (e → a) is enough here. The DP table D[i][j] for prefixes takes the cheapest of replace, delete and insert at each cell: O(n × m).
options: The number of different letters in the two words
The fewest single-letter insertions, deletions and replacements that turn one word into the other
The difference in length
The position of the first different letter

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: kitten → sitten (replace) → sittin (replace) → sitting (insert): 3. Deleting one r turns garri into gari: 1. Turning an empty string into "yam" takes three insertions, which the first row of the table encodes.

questions.q: You are designing a DP and find that the answer for a subproblem depends on the entire list of choices made so far. What does that usually mean?
questions.explain: A good state is small: amount left, parcels considered and room left, lines consumed in each text. If you need the whole history, there are as many states as histories, and DP saves nothing.
options: Use a bigger table
The state is not defined well (it should summarise what matters, like "room left"), or the problem does not have overlapping subproblems in that form
Switch to memoization
The problem is greedy

questions.q: A service memoizes knapsack answers in a module-level Map that lives as long as the process. What is the risk?
questions.explain: A memo is a cache. Inside a single computation it is released when the function returns; at module level it keeps every entry from every request forever. It can also return stale answers if the inputs it depends on change.
options: Answers become wrong after the first call
The cache grows with every distinct request and is never released: a memory leak; create the memo per call, or bound it
Maps are slower than objects
There is no risk

questions.q: What is the most convincing test for a knapsack DP?
questions.explain: Brute force is slow but obviously right on small inputs. The consistency check catches a wrong walk-back even when the number is right. Include the edges: no parcels, zero capacity, parcels heavier than the van.
options: One example from the textbook
Compare it with brute force over all subsets on many small random inputs, and check that the reconstructed parcels fit and add up to the reported value
Check that the result is positive
Time it on a large input

questions.q: A delivery robot climbs a staircase taking 1, 2 or 3 steps at a time. Write ways(n) with memoization (a Map passed down or created per call). It should print 1 2 4 7 274 for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 10.
questions.explain: The last move was 1, 2 or 3 steps, so the ways to reach n are the sum of the ways to reach n − 1, n − 2 and n − 3. Base cases: one way to stand still (n = 0), no way to be below the ground (n < 0).

questions.q: Write fewestNotes(amount, values) with a table: best[0] = 0, every other amount is 1 plus the minimum over the values, and -1 when impossible. It should print 2 3 -1 2.
questions.explain: ₦800 = 400 + 400, ₦1,200 = 400 × 3, ₦300 cannot be made from 500s and 200s (the table entry stays Infinity), and 6 = 5 + 1. The values do not need to be sorted: the table tries every value for every amount.

questions.q: Count the combinations (order does not matter) to pay an amount with the given notes, with values in the outer loop. It should print 2 10 6.
questions.explain: ways[0] = 1 (one way to pay nothing). Letting each value join in turn counts each combination once. 10 from 5, 2 and 1 has 10 combinations (for example 5+5, 5+2+2+1, 2+2+2+2+2, …).

questions.q: Write bestFee(items, capacity) for the 0/1 knapsack using a single row updated from the capacity down. It should print 160000 0 90000.
questions.explain: 5 kg: the 1 kg and 4 kg items (₦160,000). 0 kg: nothing. 3 kg: the 3 kg item alone (₦90,000) beats the 1 kg item. Going down guarantees each item is used at most once.

questions.q: Write commonLines(a, b) that returns the length of the longest common subsequence of two arrays of lines. It should print 4 0 3.
questions.explain: name, street, city and notes appear in both, in the same order; phone was deleted and landmark inserted. The first row and column are 0 because an empty list shares nothing.

questions.q: Write distance(a, b) (edit distance) and use it to suggest the closest product. It should print speakers sandals.
questions.explain: The first row and column hold the cost of building a prefix from nothing. Each cell then takes the cheapest of replace (free on a match), delete or insert. The sort compares distances, so this computes each distance several times; for many products, compute them once and sort by the stored value.

questions.q: Can the parcels be split into two vans of exactly equal weight? Use a one-row subset-sum table possible[w] up to half the total, looping down. It should print true false false.
questions.explain: 30 + 10 = 25 + 15 = 40. An odd total can never split evenly. For [100, 5, 5] the half is 55, which no subset reaches. Looping down keeps each parcel to one van.

questions.q: Which van loads are possible with parcels of 3, 5 and 7 kg (each used at most once)? What does this print?
questions.explain: The reachable totals are the sums of subsets: 0, 3, 5, 7, 3+5, 3+7, 5+7 and 3+5+7. Looping down keeps each parcel to one use; looping up would allow 3+3 = 6 and many more. The empty load (0 kg) is always possible.
